Humus is the dark, rich, spongy substance in soil that forms when dead plants, animals, and other living things completely break down over time.

When a leaf falls from a tree, or an animal dies, or grass withers — that organic material doesn't just disappear. Tiny living things like bacteria, fungi, and worms slowly eat and break it down. This process takes months or years. At the end, when the material has broken down as completely as possible, what remains is humus — a dark, soft, crumbly substance mixed into the upper layer of soil.

Think of it as nature's finished product of decomposition. It's not a fresh, rotting leaf. It's what comes after everything has fully broken down into something stable and unrecognizable from its original form.

Humus is what makes rich, healthy soil look dark brown or almost black. If you've ever dug into the ground in a forest or a well-kept garden and noticed that the top layer of soil is noticeably darker, softer, and earthy-smelling compared to the pale, hard soil below — that darker top layer is rich in humus. It has a slightly spongy, crumbly texture, and a deep, pleasant, earthy smell.
Why does humus matter so much?

Humus is incredibly important for life on Earth, for three main reasons:

1. It feeds plants. Humus is packed with nutrients — especially nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium — that plants need to grow. As humus slowly breaks down further, it releases these nutrients into the soil in a form plant roots can absorb. Soil rich in humus is fertile soil; crops and plants grow well in it.

2. It holds water. Humus acts like a sponge. It soaks up and holds water in the soil, which means plants can access moisture during dry periods. Without humus, water drains away too quickly, leaving the soil dry and unable to support plant life.

3. It improves soil structure. Humus binds tiny soil particles together into a loose, crumbly structure that has good airflow. Roots can penetrate it easily. It prevents soil from becoming hard and compacted. This structure is also what allows microorganisms — the tiny organisms that keep soil alive and healthy — to thrive.

In short, humus is the foundation of a healthy, living soil. Without it, soil becomes basically just lifeless mineral particles, and growing plants in it becomes very difficult.

Humus is found in the topsoil — the uppermost layer of the ground, usually the first few centimetres to a few dozen centimetres deep. Forests tend to have especially humus-rich soil because of the constant supply of fallen leaves, branches, and decaying matter. Poorly managed farmland, heavily built-up areas, and arid regions often have soil with very little humus, which is why they struggle to support plant life.
How does humus keep getting replenished?

Nature runs a beautiful cycle. Plants absorb nutrients from humus to grow. When those plants die, they fall to the ground and become organic matter again. Decomposers break that down, and it eventually becomes humus again — returning the nutrients to the soil for the next generation of plants. It's a continuous loop of life, death, and renewal.

Humans try to replicate this by making compost — deliberately piling up food scraps, leaves, and organic waste so it breaks down. Finished compost is close to humus and is added to garden soil to improve its quality.

These two words look nearly identical but mean completely different things and are not related to each other at all:

  • Humus (one m) → the soil substance described in this entire article.
  • Hummus (two *m*s) → the popular Middle Eastern food dip made from blended chickpeas, tahini, lemon, and garlic.

This mix-up is extremely common, so it's worth knowing.

Humus is the dark, stable, nutrient-rich organic matter in soil that forms when plant and animal material fully decomposes — and it is one of the most important substances for sustaining plant life and soil health on Earth.
